query: W melts near 3422 °C, whereas Cu boils near 2562 °C, so conventional induction or arc-plasma casting cannot readily yield a uniform W–Cu material. Phase separation and void formation can impair thermal transport. Filling a W skeleton with molten Cu or Cu powder can leave defects; spark-plasma sintering and mechanical alloying can produce finer, more uniform structures but can also leave voids; vapor-coated W powders have been sintered to achieve near-perfect contact between the constituents; and metal 3D printing has also been explored. Starting from W particles or connected W regions within a Cu matrix for heat transfer under irradiation in fusion-reactor joints, what single intervention could overcome these limitations while preserving mechanical durability? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts an outcome relative to a named existing fabrication baseline, defines the processing and service boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment and observations that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: High-pressure liquid copper infiltration of a pre‐sintered, porous tungsten scaffold will yield a nearly void‐free W–Cu composite with superior tungsten–copper interfacial bonding, thereby enhancing both thermal transport and irradiation resistance (with preserved mechanical durability) compared to conventional low-pressure or uncontrolled infiltration methods.
generation.material_initial_state: W particles or interconnected W regions embedded in a Cu matrix that exhibits phase separation, voids and incomplete interfacial contact – as typically produced by conventional infiltration, SPS, or vapor‐coating methods.
generation.intervention: Apply a high-pressure liquid Cu infiltration treatment. Melt copper (at temperatures well above its 1085 °C melting point but far below tungsten’s melting temperature) and force its penetration into a preformed porous or skeletonized tungsten structure using externally applied pressures (e.g., ≥50 MPa) in an inert (or vacuum) atmosphere.
generation.conditions: The treatment should be conducted at a processing temperature that fully melts Cu (e.g., around 1100 °C) while preserving the tungsten framework, under a controlled, high-pressure inert environment; the resulting composite is intended for fusion-reactor joint applications where it is exposed to irradiation and high thermal loads.
generation.structural_mediator: A uniform, continuous, and void-free copper phase intimately bonded to the tungsten framework, with minimal residual porosity at the W–Cu interfaces.
generation.mechanism: High external pressure boosts capillary forces to overcome the natural wettability limitations between Cu and W particles. This forces complete infiltration of the molten copper into the tungsten network, closes existing voids, minimizes phase separation during solidification, and promotes strong metallurgical bonding—features that together lower thermal interfacial resistance and resist irradiation-induced defect formation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to composites produced by conventional low-pressure methods (or those exhibiting infiltrated voids), the high-pressure infiltration composite should display improved thermal conductivity (via reduced interfacial thermal resistance) and enhanced mechanical durability under simulated fusion irradiation conditions.
generation.baseline: Conventional fabrication routes such as filling a W skeleton with molten Cu without applied pressure, spark-plasma sintering, mechanical alloying, or vapor-coating methods that can leave behind voids/defects and phase separation limiting performance under irradiation.
generation.boundary: Processing must remain below tungsten’s melting point (3422 °C) and above copper’s (1085 °C), with the applied pressure and inert atmosphere within ranges that do not induce microstructural damage; service conditions are those relevant to heat-transferring fusion-reactor joints under irradiation.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvements in thermal conductivity and irradiation resistance are uncertain and require experimental validation. Optimization of pressure levels and dwell times may be needed to balance complete infiltration with avoidance of pressure-induced damage.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of W–Cu composite samples: one set fabricated via conventional low-pressure infiltration and the other via the proposed high-pressure liquid Cu infiltration process. Characterize both sets using high-resolution SEM/TEM to quantify void fraction and interfacial contact. Additionally, measure thermal conductivity and perform irradiation tests (e.g., using ion beams to simulate fusion conditions) to assess mechanical durability and thermal transport performance.
measurements: Void fraction and interfacial bonding quality (SEM/TEM imaging)
Mechanical properties before and after irradiation (e.g., microhardness, tensile tests)
Irradiation-induced defect density and microstructural evolution (TEM post-irradiation)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high-pressure infiltration samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in void content (e.g., <20% improvement), nor an improvement of at least 20% in thermal conductivity and mechanical durability (post-irradiation strength and fracture resistance) compared to conventional samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.
